articles.title: Association between the use of traditional Chinese medicine patterns as an inclusion criterion and statistical significance in primary outcomes of randomized placebo-controlled trials of Chinese herbal formulas.
articles.abstract: Randomized, placebo-controlled trials of Chinese herbal formulas (CHFs) are commonly used to evaluate efficacy, but a proportion of such trials fail to demonstrate statistically significant effects on primary outcomes. Some researchers have pointed out that excluding traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) pattern differentiation from inclusion criteria may reduce the alignment between treatment and enrolled patient characteristics, which could, in turn, affect observed efficacy. This study analyzed 378 randomized, placebo-controlled trials of CHFs with clearly defined primary outcomes that were published between January 1, 2020, and October 21, 2025, and identified through searches of eight databases. A total of 92,691 participants were included in the primary outcome analyses. Of these, 324 trials (85.7%) reported statistically significant results on primary outcomes, and 197 (52.1%) used TCM patterns as an inclusion criterion. Multivariable Poisson regression revealed that trials using TCM patterns were more likely to report statistically significant results (adjusted risk ratio [aRR] = 1.14; 95% CI: 1.06-1.23; P = 0.001). The association was generally consistent across prespecified subgroups and sensitivity analyses; however, only 52 studies (13.8%) were evaluated as low risk of bias according to the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 tool. Because this study included only published trials and few published pattern-based trials reported statistically nonsignificant primary outcomes, the observed association should be interpreted cautiously and may be influenced by publication bias, selective outcome reporting, and contextual differences in research and reporting practices. Further high-quality, prospectively registered, methodologically rigorous, and better-standardized trials are needed to evaluate this association.

articles.title: Evaluating the Association Between PPI Use and Dementia Risk Considering Methodological Choices: An Updated Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), commonly prescribed for gastrointestinal disorders, have been investigated for their association with the risk of dementia. We aimed to assess the association between PPI use and dementia risk in older adults and examine the influence of methodological choices on this association. We conducted a meta-analysis of longitudinal observational studies, including subgroup analyses to address time-related biases and comparator selection. Relevant studies were systematically searched in the MEDLINE, Embase, and CENTRAL databases from their inception to January 25, 2026. Twenty-three studies of older adults without dementia at baseline, reporting adjusted estimates for PPI users versus a comparator group, met the inclusion criteria. The pooled hazard ratio (HR) indicated a modest association between PPI use and dementia (HR = 1.18, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.02-1.37). Dementia risk did not differ significantly between PPI users and users of histamine-2 receptor antagonists (H2RAs) (HR = 1.04, 95% CI 0.89-1.20). In a post hoc analysis, H2RA use itself was associated with dementia (HR = 1.44, 95% CI 1.07-1.93), whereas excluding H2RA-treated patients strengthened the PPI estimate (HR = 1.75, 95% CI 1.38-2.22). Estimates also differed according to how time-related bias was handled: lag time, HR = 1.25, 95% CI 1.07-1.46; time-varying exposure, HR = 1.38, 95% CI 1.16-1.64. PPI use was modestly associated with incident dementia. However, the strength and specificity depended substantially on comparator selection and handling of time-related bias. Well-designed, long-term studies using active comparators are needed to clarify whether this effect is PPI-specific.

articles.title: Engineering human brain microphysiological systems for alzheimer's disease (AD) and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) modeling and drug testing: translational promise, limitations, and future directions.
articles.abstract: This review examines the emerging role of human brain microphysiological systems (HBMPS) in recapitulating diseases and evaluating their translational potential and limitations for Alzheimer's disease (AD) and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). Both disorders differ in underlying cause, but converge on shared downstream pathophysiology such as tau pathology, neuroinflammation, and blood-brain barrier (BBB) dysfunction. We review the critical pathophysiological features relevant to modeling AD and CTE and introduce HBMPS platforms/validation strategies as potential tools for evaluating therapeutic compounds as well as drug-delivery approaches. We also provide a systematic comparison of the relative advantages and disadvantages of 2D, HBMPS, Xenograft, and animal models and discuss the future potential of HBMPS's drug-testing platform. We further discuss current challenges of HBMPS related to drug testing, engineering extracellular matrix for tissue chips, and BBB penetration in AD and CTE. We suggest future integration of organoid xenografts and AI-assisted frameworks to enhance pathophysiological fidelity/drug predictive capability and to bridge the gap between HBMPS and animal models. In summary, this paper reviews HBMPS technologies as future translation platforms' direction for drug screening and delivery, while providing current limitations and challenges including model validation, reproducibility, and standardized regulatory bases required for preclinical success for HBMPS use. Rather than comparing biological complexity with translational validity, this review applies a decision-oriented framework that distinguishes mechanistic fidelity, comparative candidate ranking, predictive validation, investigational new drug (IND)-supporting use, and replacement of a defined animal test. For each use, we identify quantitative transport, exposure-response, pharmacodynamic, safety, and reproducibility evidence required to support an advance, redesign, or go/stop decision.

articles.title: Lysosome-targeted nanomaterials for advanced cancer therapy: Overcoming resistance, activating immunity and amplifying therapeutic synergy.
articles.abstract: Lysosomes were once regarded merely as the cellular "waste disposal" system, but are now widely recognized as pivotal hubs for regulating intracellular homeostasis and have emerged as promising therapeutic targets in cancer treatment. This review systematically explores the interplay between nanomaterials and lysosomal function, focusing particularly on how to leverage this interaction to enhance antitumor efficacy. First, we outline the mechanisms by which nanomaterials modulate lysosomal activity. Next, we review the main antitumor pathways used by lysosome-targeted nanomaterials, such as inhibiting autophagic flux, activating programmed cell death pathways (including cuproptosis, ferroptosis, apoptosis, and pyroptosis), and remodeling the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. We also analyze various strategies for synergistic enhancement, such as metabolic intervention and stimuli-responsive combination therapies (such as light-, ultrasound- or ROS-activated), as well as lysosome-targeted approaches for improving conventional chemotherapy and radiotherapy. In conclusion, this review provides a comprehensive overview of current lysosome-targeted nanomedicine research and outlines future directions for translating these strategies into clinical applications.

articles.title: Emerging insights into PPARα's role in lean metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease: Implications for targeted therapies.
articles.abstract: Lean metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), defined as hepatic steatosis in individuals with normal BMI (<25 kg/m2 in non-Asians; <23 kg/m2 in Asians), is a clinically paradoxical phenotype in which patients face risks of progressive fibrosis, cardiovascular events, and liver-related mortality comparable to or exceeding obese counterparts. Visceral adiposity, dietary stressors, cholesterol overload, and genetic susceptibility involving PNPLA3 variants and PPARA polymorphisms synergistically disrupt hepatic lipid homeostasis. At the core of this dysregulation lies peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARα), a master transcriptional regulator of hepatic fatty acid oxidation, ketogenesis, and anti-inflammatory signaling. PPARα suppression aries through convergent mechanisms, including aging-related RAGE signaling, fructose-mediated epigenetic silencing, gut‒liver axis disruption, and lipotoxicity, operating independently of systemic obesity. This review demonstrates that: (1) impaired PPARα activity underlies lean MASLD pathogenesis through transcriptional, epigenetic, and post-translational suppression; (2) synthetic PPARα agonists show limited applicability in this metabolically fragile population; and (3) natural product-derived modulators engage PPARα alongside FXR and LXR networks to restore metabolic balance. The PPARα-FGF21-ketogenesis axis and nuclear receptor crosstalk provide the mechanistic rationale for network-level therapeutic approaches. We advocate for spatially selective hepatic PPARα reactivation guided by lean-specific biomarker and genotype-stratified trial design.

articles.title: Antibody peptide conjugates as multifunctional therapeutics: Mechanisms, challenges, and prospects.
articles.abstract: Antibody peptide conjugates (APCs) represent a newly emerging class of targeted biotherapeutics that embody a novel structural paradigm by combining the precise targeting capabilities of antibodies with the versatile biological functions of peptides. APCs not only overcome the inherent limitations of conventional peptide therapeutics but also go beyond the cytotoxicity-focused paradigm of traditional antibody drug conjugates (ADCs). By flexibly combining peptide payload activities with antibody functions, APCs have developed into diverse therapeutic strategies, including immunomodulation, targeted antibacterial, and targeted protein degradation, among others. Several APCs have already achieved notable progress and entered clinical studies, underscoring their potential as a next-generation targeted therapeutic platform. In this review, we present the first comprehensive structural framework for APCs, defining seven distinct subtypes and discussing their biological mechanisms, structure-activity relationships, recent advances, and major challenges. Furthermore, we propose guiding principles for the rational design of APCs and highlight future research directions, aiming to accelerate progress in this rapidly developing field of innovative therapeutics.

articles.title: Application of computational methods in the drug discovery and development of Alzheimer's disease.
articles.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a prevalent neurodegenerative disorder marked by the accumulation of amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles in the brain, leading to cognitive decline. As the most common dementia, AD affects over 50 million individuals worldwide, with 10 million new cases each year. Despite many significant progresses in AD research fields, there is still no effective treatment. Advances in molecular modelling and artificial intelligence (AI) algorithm have facilitated the application of computational methods in AD drug development, offering advantages in terms of efficiency, cost-effectiveness, and resource conservation. These strategies, including molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, protein structure prediction, virtual screening, and de novo drug design, have been widely employed in the past decades. Additionally, AI pharmaceutical companies have revolutionized the traditional drug development pipeline such as AD biomarker discovery, accurate diagnosis and precision medicine, etc. This review offers a thorough summary of recent progresses in computational-based methodologies in the study of AD drug development, including the elucidation the pathological mechanism at the molecular level, target identification, target 3D structure prediction, lead compound discovery, de novo molecular generation, multi-target directed ligands, drug repurposing, biomarker discovery, etc., showing promising applications of molecular modelling and AI in the development of AD therapy.

articles.title: Advances and perspectives of next-generation antitumor antibody-based modalities: Structural innovation and target-driven strategies.
articles.abstract: Antibody-based therapies have gained significant traction in oncology, as evidenced by their prominent presence at international conferences such as American Association for Cancer Research (AACR) and American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO). Modalities including antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs), bispecific antibodies (BsAbs), and T-cell engagers (TCEs) are increasingly recognized as pillars of precision medicine. Driven by advances in molecular engineering, antibody formats and mechanisms of action have evolved beyond conventional antigen blockade to encompass multimodal cytotoxicity and immune modulation. ADCs now leverage optimized linkers and payloads for targeted delivery and potent tumor cell killing. BsAbs simultaneously engage tumor and immune cell targets to enhance immune activation, while TCEs enable T cells to recognize intracellular antigens presented via MHC, overcoming the limitations of extracellular targeting. Emerging design strategies are increasingly tailored to target-specific features such as expression levels, internalization capacity, and cellular subtype. Innovations include non-internalizing ADCs for low-abundance targets and biased antibody architectures that preferentially activate CD8+ T cells. These developments are expanding the therapeutic landscape toward greater efficacy, safety, and personalization. This review outlines the global landscape of antibody drug development, highlighting a paradigm shift toward target-driven design principles that integrate structural innovation with functional precision.

articles.title: The interaction of flavonoids, alkaloids, and terpenoids with the major drug transporters in the organic anion transporting polypeptide and organic anion transporter families.
articles.abstract: Natural compounds are ubiquitously found in the plant kingdom and are well-known for their beneficial effects on human health. The easy accessibility and the relatively affordable price make them popular choices for self-medication and/or as part of a healthy daily diet. While it has long been established that natural compounds can influence the function of drug transporters, information about these interactions is often scattered and fragmented. To more systematically and comprehensively summarize the available information in the related field, we categorized the natural products that affect uptake transporters in the organic anion transporting polypeptide (OATP) and organic anion transporter (OAT) families into three groups: flavonoids, alkaloids, and terpenoids. By providing the half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) and/or inhibition constant (K i) of the specific substrates and comparing them to the maximum plasma concentrations (C max) of natural products, the likelihood of drug-drug interactions (DDIs) at these transporters is proposed. Moreover, information regarding mechanistic studies, which is essential for understanding the molecular mechanisms of natural product-transporter interactions but is currently quite limited, is included. We also suggested potential indirect DDIs posed by natural compounds that are mediated by nuclear receptors and protein kinases, which may affect expression and post-translational modification of OATPs and OATs.

articles.title: Modulating macrophage efferocytosis: Drug delivery strategies for enhancement, mimicry, and inhibition.
articles.abstract: Efferocytosis, the non-inflammatory clearance of apoptotic cells, is essential for tissue homeostasis and inflammation resolution. Efferocytosis has different effects in the context of different diseases, providing a compelling therapeutic target. Impaired efferocytosis is linked to the progression of cardiovascular, autoimmune, and neurological disorders, whereas in tumors, efferocytosis often facilitates immunosuppression and metastasis. This review comprehensively summarizes recent advances in drug delivery systems (DDSs) designed for the modulation of macrophage efferocytosis. We first introduce the mechanisms of efferocytosis and its pathophysiological roles across diseases. Next, we thoroughly review DDSs designed to enhance, mimic, or inhibit efferocytosis, with a particular focus on various targeting methods to achieve precise efferocytosis modulation. Finally, we discuss translational challenges and propose future perspectives for efferocytosis-targeting therapies. This work aims to provide a foundational reference for the rational design of efferocytosis-modulating delivery systems and to underscore their therapeutic potential in a range of diseases.

articles.title: Post CDK4/6 inhibitors: Novel targeted combinations based on SERDs in HR+/HER2- advanced breast cancer.
articles.abstract: The addition of cyclin-dependent kinase 4 and 6 (CDK4/6) inhibitors to endocrine therapy has redefined the treatment paradigm for HR-positive, HER2-negative (HR+/HER2-) advanced breast cancer, with clear survival gains. However, resistance is almost inevitable and remains the central barrier to durable benefit. Selective estrogen receptor degraders (SERDs) have therefore moved from a later-line option to a core component of post-progression strategies aimed at targeting ESR1 mutations and estrogen receptor (ER) pathway reactivation. Notably, oral SERDs differ substantially in ER occupancy, degradation potency, and pharmacokinetic behavior, and these differences appear to translate into distinct efficacy and toxicity profiles across studies. This review summarizes recent progress in SERD-based therapeutic strategies, with a focus on post-CDK4/6 inhibitor sequencing and biomarker-driven combination approaches. Particular attention is given to rational combinations with PI3Kα and AKT inhibitors, HER2-directed tyrosine kinase inhibitors, and emerging targets such as FGFR, CDK2, and CDK7, as well as the growing role of liquid biopsy in guiding treatment adaptation. Together, these developments position SERD-centered strategies as a key framework for advancing mechanism-informed, precision treatment in HR+/HER2- advanced breast cancer.

articles.title: Mapping neutrophil membrane bioactivity to therapeutic interfaces: Biology, disease targeting, and activity-guided biomimetic therapy.
articles.abstract: Neutrophil plasma membranes encode a tightly coordinated set of bioactivities that control inflammatory trafficking, endothelial adhesion under shear, effector activation, and immune regulation. In this review, we present a membrane-centric framework that conceptualizes the neutrophil membrane as a programmable therapeutic interface integrating targeting, adhesion, and effector regulation. We delineate core membrane modules-including chemokine-sensing G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), selectin ligands, β2 integrins, Fcγ and complement receptors, pattern-recognition receptors (PRRs), and lipid-raft microdomains-and examine how their coordinated dynamics govern tissue targeting, adhesion kinetics, effector thresholds, and resolution. Integrating evidence from infection, sterile inflammation, autoimmunity, and cancer, we highlight how dysregulated membrane programs drive pathology, while their selective tuning enables therapeutic benefit. Building on this biology, we discuss two convergent intervention strategies: direct pharmacological modulation of neutrophil membrane signaling axes, and activity-guided engineering of neutrophil membrane-derived therapeutics, including native vesicles and membrane-coated nanomaterials. We further link key engineering parameters-such as membrane orientation, ligand density, glycan architecture, and microdomain integrity-to mechanism-based potency, safety, and translational control. By positioning the neutrophil membrane as a programmable interface rather than a static biomimetic shell, this review outlines a rational roadmap for developing predictable, dose-controlled therapies for infection, inflammatory diseases, and cancer.

articles.title: Molecular mechanisms, crosstalk and therapeutic potential of novel acylation modifications in cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases.
articles.abstract: Metabolic reprogramming, the fundamental process by which cells adapt to fluctuations in energy demands, is pivotal in the pathophysiology of cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases (CCVDs). Aberrant reprogramming of glucose, lipid, and amino acid metabolism is intricately associated with pathological processes in CCVDs such as cardiac hypertrophy, atherosclerosis, and ischemia-reperfusion injury. This metabolic remodeling disrupts the dynamic balance of metabolites (cc, acetyl-CoA and lactate) in the cardio-cerebrovascular systems, thereby inducing abnormal post-translational modifications (PTMs) on histones and non-histone proteins. These PTMs drive disease progression by modulating gene transcription or the activity of key proteins, which subsequently influences downstream signaling pathways. Here, we systematically examine the regulatory enzymes and functional roles of nine recently characterized acylation modifications: crotonylation, β-hydroxybutyrylation, 2-hydroxyisobutyrylation, succinylation, malonylation, glutarylation, lactylation, propionylation, and butyrylation. Furthermore, this review elaborates on the molecular mechanisms, crosstalk and the latest preclinical advancements regarding these acylations in CCVDs, emphasizing the influence of distinct acylation patterns on various pathological processes and highlighting the clinical translational prospects of targeting these novel modifications for therapeutic intervention.

articles.title: Antibody‒cell conjugates: A novel "off-the-shelf" modality bridging ADCs and CAR-T for cancer immunotherapy.
articles.abstract: Antibody‒cell conjugates (ACCs) represent a promising therapeutic strategy emerging in the biopharmaceutical industry to overcome the limitations of current immunotherapies. ACCs constitute a novel class of living drugs developed by anchoring functional antibodies onto the surface of living cells via specific linkers or conjugation methods. These carrier cells encompass both immune effector cells (such as Natural Killer cells, γδ T cells, and activated T cells) and non-immune cells (such as erythrocytes and platelets). Distinct from genetic engineering, ACCs directly modify the cell surface using chemical biology, enzymatic catalysis, or physical assembly, thereby endowing cells with precise tumor-targeting capabilities while preserving their intrinsic biological functions. This technology facilitates the scalable production of "off-the-shelf" therapeutics and has shown promising potential in treating both hematological malignancies and refractory solid tumors with a superior safety profile. This review systematically examines the current construction strategies and carrier cell selection for ACCs, covering both immune effector cells and non-immune carrier cells, and discusses the clinical progress, key challenges, and future directions.

articles.title: Intelligent nano delivery systems: Classification, stimuli-responsive mechanisms, and therapeutic applications in critical illnesses.
articles.abstract: Critical illnesses such as sepsis and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) evolve rapidly and are dominated by systemic inflammatory dysregulation, oxidative stress, and abrupt microenvironmental remodeling, which collectively narrow the therapeutic window and amplify treatment-related toxicity. Conventional pharmacotherapy is often limited by non-selective biodistribution, insufficient lesion exposure, and dose-limiting adverse effects. Intelligent nano-delivery systems (INDS) address these barriers by coupling pathological cues (e.g., pH gradients, redox/ROS imbalance, and disease-associated enzymes) to defined carrier-state transitions, thereby enabling lesion-confined activation, controlled bioavailability, and, in selected designs, real-time readouts. In this review, we summarize the design logic of stimulus-responsive and targeting modules, and critically discuss how they translate endogenous signals into payload release or functional actuation in representative critical-illness settings. We further highlight emerging directions, including self-adaptive multi-input gating and biomimetic interfaces, and discuss key translational constraints (manufacturability, safety, and reproducibility) that must be addressed to advance INDS toward critical-care practice.

articles.title: Potassium-Competitive Acid Blockers in GERD and Helicobacter pylori Infection: The Emerging Role of Fexuprazan.
articles.abstract: The pharmacological control of gastric acid secretion has evolved substantially over the past five decades, yet clinically important limitations remain with delayed-release proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), including delayed onset of action, meal dependency, nocturnal acid breakthrough, and variable intragastric pH control. Potassium-competitive acid blockers (P-CABs) represent a major advance in antisecretory therapy by providing rapid, potent, sustained, and meal-independent inhibition of the gastric H+,K+-ATPase through a reversible mechanism of action. Among currently available P-CABs, fexuprazan is a relatively recent agent for which an expanding body of pharmacological and clinical evidence has become available. This review critically examines its pharmacology, experimental biology, and clinical efficacy, with particular emphasis on gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and Helicobacter pylori infection. Randomized controlled trials and real-world studies demonstrate that fexuprazan is non-inferior to esomeprazole in healing erosive esophagitis, with evidence of rapid symptom improvement, effective nocturnal symptom control, and greater dosing flexibility. Emerging data also suggest potential benefit in extra-esophageal manifestations of GERD. Experimental studies indicate anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and epithelial barrier-protective properties, although their clinical relevance remains to be established. In H. pylori infection, the profound and sustained intragastric pH elevation achieved with P-CABs may enhance eradication therapy, and fexuprazan-based triple, quadruple, and dual regimens have shown promising efficacy and tolerability. Overall, current evidence indicates that fexuprazan is an effective and well-tolerated P-CAB that may overcome some of the limitations of conventional PPIs, while ongoing comparative and long-term studies will further define its place in the management of acid-related disorders.

articles.title: Short-course versus standard- or longer-course oral antibiotic therapy for pneumonia and lower respiratory tract infection in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Reducing unnecessary antibiotic exposure is a major priority in pediatric antimicrobial stewardship. The comparative effectiveness of short-course versus standard- or longer-course oral antibiotic therapy for uncomplicated bacterial infections in children remains uncertain. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate whether short-course oral antibiotic therapy increases clinical treatment failure compared with standard- or longer-course therapy in children with uncomplicated bacterial infections, with a primary focus on same-antibiotic pediatric pneumonia/lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) trials. METHODS: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and CENTRAL were searched, supplemented by citation searching and trial registry review. Eligible studies enrolled children aged 0-18 years with uncomplicated bacterial infections treated with oral antibiotics in outpatient or ambulatory settings. The primary outcome was clinical treatment failure; broader pneumonia/LRTI and all-infection analyses were treated as sensitivity or exploratory analyses. Random-effects meta-analysis used risk ratios (RRs) and risk differences (RDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool. The review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261339263). RESULTS: Fourteen randomized trials were included; nine same-antibiotic pneumonia/LRTI comparisons contributed to the primary pooled analysis. Short-course therapy was not associated with increased treatment failure (RR, 1.01; 95% CI, 0.92-1.11; I2 = 0.0%), and the absolute-effect analysis showed no meaningful difference (RD, 0.001; 95% CI, -0.010 to 0.013; I2 = 10.0%). A broad pneumonia/LRTI sensitivity analysis including different-antibiotic comparisons was also non-significant (RR, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.66-1.33) but heterogeneous. The all-infection exploratory analysis was similarly non-significant (RR, 0.89; 95% CI, 0.63-1.25) and interpreted cautiously given clinical heterogeneity. Of the 14 trials, 5 were at low risk of bias, 2 had some concerns, and 7 were at high risk. CONCLUSION: In same-antibiotic pediatric pneumonia/LRTI trials, short-course therapy was not associated with increased clinical treatment failure compared with standard- or longer-course therapy. Broader analyses across different antibiotic strategies and infection syndromes did not materially change this interpretation but showed substantial heterogeneity. These findings support cautious, infection-specific antibiotic duration reduction rather than broad generalization across all uncomplicated pediatric bacterial infections. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261339263, identifier CRD420261339263.

articles.title: Continuous infusion versus intermittent infusion of vancomycin: a systematic review and meta-analysis with a focus on nephrotoxicity, target attainment, and clinical outcomes.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Vancomycin is widely used for Gram-positive infections but has a narrow therapeutic window and significant nephrotoxicity risk. Whether continuous infusion (CI) offers advantages over intermittent infusion (II) remains debated. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to compare CI versus II vancomycin regarding nephrotoxicity, target attainment, clinical outcomes, and time to therapeutic target. METHODS: PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were searched from inception to March 2026. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies comparing CI and II of vancomycin were included. Outcomes assessed were nephrotoxicity, target concentration attainment, clinical efficacy, microbiological clearance, mortality, and time to therapeutic target. Pooled odds ratios (ORs) or mean differences (MDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using random-effects models. RESULTS: A total of 23 studies comprising 3,053 patients were included. CI was associated with significantly reduced nephrotoxicity (OR = 0.62, 95% CI = 0.48-0.79, I2 = 42%), higher target attainment (OR = 2.85, 95% CI = 2.12-3.84, I2 = 38%), and shorter time to therapeutic target (MD = -1.52 days, 95% CI = -1.98 to -1.06, I2 = 67%). No significant differences were observed for clinical efficacy (OR = 1.12, 95% CI = 0.86-1.46), microbiological clearance (OR = 1.08, 95% CI = 0.72-1.62), or mortality (OR = 0.94, 95% CI = 0.71-1.25). CONCLUSION: Continuous infusion of vancomycin reduces nephrotoxicity risk, improves target attainment, and shortens time to therapeutic target compared with intermittent infusion, without compromising clinical efficacy or survival. These findings support CI as a preferred strategy in patients at heightened risk of renal injury. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261365683, identifier CRD420261365683.

articles.title: Benefit-risk profiling of advanced therapies in moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis: a clustered network meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: The therapeutic landscape for moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis (UC) has expanded with the introduction of oral small molecules and recently approved biologics. However, the scarcity of head-to-head trials necessitates indirect comparisons to clarify their relative positioning. We aimed to determine the comparative efficacy and tolerability hierarchy of approved and emerging advanced therapies, incorporating the most contemporary evidence. METHODS: We retrieved randomized controlled trials (RCTs) from major databases up to November 2025. Efficacy outcomes included clinical remission and endoscopic improvement; tolerability was evaluated via discontinuations due to adverse events. We employed Bayesian network meta-analysis and bivariate clustered ranking to visualize efficacy-tolerability profiles, stratifying by prior biologic exposure. RESULTS: A total of 32 RCTs were included. In the induction phase, Upadacitinib, Ustekinumab, and Risankizumab co-occupied the "most favorable" quadrant, combining high efficacy with superior tolerability. In the maintenance phase, Upadacitinib 30 mg demonstrated the highest-ranking probability for efficacy, while IL-23 antagonists (Guselkumab, Mirikizumab) and low-dose Upadacitinib exhibited a highly favorable efficacy-tolerability profile. Notably, in biologic-exposed patients, Upadacitinib demonstrated the highest relative efficacy among evaluated therapies, whereas Guselkumab emerged as a highly effective biologic alternative based on current estimates. CONCLUSION: Based on current network estimates, Upadacitinib is suggested among the most efficacious options for achieving clinical and endoscopic endpoints, particularly in refractory disease, while IL-23 antagonists present highly favorable tolerability profiles for maintenance without compromising efficacy. These findings support a tailored approach to drug selection, aligning patient-specific profiles of inflammatory burden with current evidence-based safety thresholds. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261292029, identifier CRD420261292029.

articles.title: Nanoarchitectonics via emulsion interfacial in situ polymerization for enhanced cross-presentation and antitumor immunity.
articles.abstract: Emulsion adjuvants enhance vaccine responses by forming antigen reservoirs and maintaining local immune stimulation, but their dynamic oil-water interfaces have limitations in regulating intracellular transport and cross-presentation. Here, we developed a mild in situ emulsion interface polymerization (EIIP) strategy, utilizing the oil-water interface as a confined reaction zone to generate functional polymer shells around the antigen-containing droplets. By constructing particles with consistent components, the same antigen is confined to the aqueous core or on the shell surface respectively, thereby evaluating the contribution of antigen location to immunity. Internal compartmentalization enhanced dendritic-cell maturation and MHC-I cross presentation. It retained antigen within the pH-responsive shell during intracellular trafficking, which triggered mitochondrial perturbation, cytosolic mitochondrial DNA accumulation and increased 2'3'-cGAMP. In vivo, internal antigen compartmentalization strengthened antigen-specific CD8+ T cell responses and antitumour efficacy. EIIP retains the squalene emulsion, which prolonged antigen retention at the injection site and promoted delivery to draining lymph nodes. The distinct contributions of squalene in prophylactic and therapeutic tumor models further indicate that prolonged antigen exposure and antigen localization are non-equivalent determinants of vaccine activity. EIIP turns the emulsion interface into a reaction zone, thereby alters its cross-presentation and antigen-specific CD8+ T cell response.

articles.title: Tetrahedral DNA engineered Janus nanoplatform for potentiated Zn2+ interference therapy and cGAS-STING activation via efficient delivery of exogenous DNA.
articles.abstract: While zinc-ion interference therapy presents a compelling approach for cancer immunotherapy, poor intracellular bioavailability and weak innate immune activation restrict its therapeutic potential. To overcome these bottlenecks, we developed tetrahedral DNA-integrated ZnFe2O4-ZnO Janus nanoparticles (TDN-ZIZJP) to achieve spatiotemporal modulation of immunity. Distinct from conventional cubic nanoparticles, this nail-shaped Janus architecture amplifies cell-particle interactions, substantially improving tumor penetration and cellular uptake. This unique feature endows improved selectively dissolving of ZnO domain within the mildly acidic tumor microenvironment, resulting in a targeted intracellular surge of Zn2+. This enhanced ion flux provokes oxidative stress and endogenous DNA damage, thereby increasing the availability of endogenous cytosolic DNA. Moreover, the integrated tetrahedral DNA nanostructures serve as a robust reservoir, delivering abundant exogenous dsDNA directly into the cytoplasm. Zn2+-induced endogenous DNA release and TDN-derived exogenous dsDNA jointly increase the availability of cytosolic DNA substrates for cGAS. This dual-source DNA supply supports sustained cGAS-STING activation, thereby enhancing type I interferon signaling, promoting dendritic cell maturation and increasing cytotoxic T-cell infiltration. This study provides a new avenue that couples Zn2+-mediated ion interference and endogenous DNA damage with an exogenous dsDNA reservoir, providing a highly tunable platform for metal ion-regulated immunotherapy.

articles.title: Shugan Xiaozhi Formula Reduces Hepatic Steatosis and Stiffness in MASLD Patients with Elevated ALT: An Exploratory 24-Week Randomized Trial.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Metabolic dysfunction-related fatty liver disease (MASLD) affects approximately one-third of adults worldwide. The most common manifestations in the early stage are liver dysfunction, hepatic steatosis，metabolic abnormalities, and obesity. The failure of single behavioral interventions and the limited availability of treatment drugs remain unmet clinical needs. METHODS: In this 24-week, multicenter, prospective, randomized, open-label, active-controlled, proof-of-concept trial conducted in China, 285 participants with MASLD (ALT >40U/L to 5×ULN) were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive Shugan Xiaozhi Formula (SGXZ) granules or vitamin E 300mg/day. The primary exploratory endpoints were changes in hepatic steatosis measured by MRI-proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF) and FibroScan-controlled attenuation parameter (CAP), and changes in liver stiffness by transient elastography (TE) and magnetic resonance elastography (MRE). Additional outcomes included liver enzymes, anthropometric measures, and safety parameters. Analyses were performed in the completer population (n=152) using ANCOVA and logistic regression. RESULTS: At week 24, SGXZ significantly reduced MRI-PDFF (adjusted mean difference vs vitamin E, -3.44 percentage points; 95% CI, -5.18 to -1.69; P<0.001) and CAP (-45.42dB/m; 95% CI, -58.37 to -32.47; P<0.001). A higher proportion of SGXZ recipients achieved a ≥1-category reduction in MRI-PDFF-defined steatosis grade (22.4% vs 5.3%; OR, 5.83; P=0.007) and a ≥30dB/m reduction in CAP (82.9% vs 39.5%; OR, 8.01; P<0.001). Liver stiffness parameters also improved more with SGXZ (TE, -1.14 kPa; P<0.001; MRE, -0.06m/s; P<0.001). Changes in ALT and AST did not differ between groups, whereas GGT normalization was more frequent with SGXZ (52.3% vs 27.7%; OR, 2.87; P=0.010). SGXZ was also associated with significantly greater reductions in body weight (between-group mean difference, -2.69kg; 95% CI, -3.60 to -1.78; P < 0.001), BMI (-0.94kg/m²; 95% CI, -1.26 to -0.62; P < 0.001), and WHR (-0.04; 95% CI, -0.08 to -0.01; P = 0.020). SGXZ was generally well tolerated; gastrointestinal events were more common but were mild and self-limiting. No serious adverse events or clinically meaningful laboratory safety signals occurred. CONCLUSIONS: In this exploratory trial, SGXZ was associated with greater reductions in hepatic steatosis, imaging-based liver stiffness, body weight, BMI, and WHR than vitamin E, with an acceptable safety profile. These findings suggest that SGXZ represents a highly promising compound natural medicine therapeutic option for the complex metabolic diseases MASLD/MASH. It meets the urgent clinical need for safe and effective therapies to comprehensively improve patients' conditions. Of course, these findings require further validation in large-scale trials with sufficient statistical power. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: ChiCTR2200057595.

articles.title: Targeting the Catalytic and ZnF-UBP Domains of HDAC6 Differentially Controls NLRP3 Inflammasome Priming and Assembly in Paclitaxel-Induced Peripheral Neuropathy.
articles.abstract: Paclitaxel-induced peripheral neuropathy (PIPN) is a dose-limiting complication of cancer chemotherapy driven by macrophage-mediated NLRP3 inflammasome activation. While suppressing TLR-NF-κB-dependent priming can limit neuroinflammation by reducing both NLRP3 induction and downstream inflammasome activation, such upstream intervention may also affect broader immune transcriptional programs in vulnerable oncology patients. Here, we identify a structural division of labor within histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6) that pharmacologically uncouples the priming and assembly steps of NLRP3 activation. In a murine PIPN model, we demonstrate that paclitaxel directly primes macrophages. Complementary ND7/23-BMDM experiments support a model in which ATP released from paclitaxel-stressed neuronal cells provides a second signal for inflammasome assembly. By integrating domain-selective pharmacology with genetic knockdown-rescue using catalytically inactive and ZnF-UBP-deletion mutants, we reveal that the catalytic domain of HDAC6 governs upstream TLR4-NF-κB-dependent priming. In contrast, the non-catalytic ZnF-UBP domain is required for downstream HDAC6-NLRP3-ASC complexation and ASC speck assembly, ultimately driving caspase-1 activation, GSDMD cleavage, and IL-1β release. In vivo, targeting the ZnF-UBP domain with CP31 effectively alleviated paclitaxel-evoked pain hypersensitivity and dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neuroinflammation without altering canonical α-tubulin acetylation. By reframing HDAC6 into domain-separable intervention points, we provide a pathway-restricted therapeutic strategy for PIPN that precisely disarms downstream pathological inflammasome assembly while largely preserving the measured upstream priming responses.

articles.title: Striatofugal balance and beneficial effects of facilitating nucleus accumbens mGlu4 receptor activity in the Fmr1-/- mouse model of Fragile X Syndrome.
articles.abstract: Fragile X Syndrome (FXS) is the leading monogenic cause of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). To date, no approved pharmacological treatment alleviates social impairments in patients with FXS. Since D1 and D2 dopamine receptor-expressing striatal projection neurons (SPNs) were shown to regulate ASD-sensitive behaviors, we explored whether the balance of activity between D1- and D2-SPNs would be biased in the Fmr1-/- mouse model of FXS. We evaluated striatal function in Fmr1-/- and Fmr1+/+ mice under pharmacological challenge and performed RNAscope® in situ hybridization following social interaction to assess the activity of SPNs in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) and dorsal striatum (DS). We evidenced a decrease in D1-SPN activity, biasing the D1/D2-SPN balance. We then evaluated the effects of compounds developed to repress D2-SPN activity on behavioral impairments in Fmr1-/- mice. Systemically facilitating mGlu4 or blocking A2a receptor activity relieved behavioral deficits in this model. Moreover, social interaction in Fmr1-/- mice was fully rescued by photopharmacological activation of mGlu4 in the ventral pallidum, to which both NAc D1- and D2-SPNs project, and mGlu4 receptors in the NAc likely contributed to restoring social deficits after systemic mGlu4 facilitation. Together, these results are consistent with our working hypotheses of both biased striatal D1/D2-SPN balance in social deficit and contribution of mGlu4 receptors expressed by NAc SPNs in modulating social behavior. In conclusion, pharmacological compounds able to regulate SPN activity demonstrate a promising therapeutic potential to relieve ASD-like deficits in FXS. PHARMACOLOGICAL COMPOUNDS: ADX88178 (CAS 1235318-89-4); haloperidol hydrochloride (CAS 1511-16-6); istradefylline (CAS 155270-99-8); LSP4-2022 (CAS 1413405-33-0); morphine hydrochloride (CAS 6055-06-7); quinpirole hydrochloride (CAS 85798-08-9); SCH-23390 hydrochloride (CAS 125941-87-9); SKF-81297 hydrobromide (CAS 67287-39-2); sulpiride (CAS 15676-16-1); VU0155041 sodium (CAS 1259372-69-4); optogluram (CAS 1627840-48-5).

articles.title: GLP-1 receptor activation attenuates chronic migraine-like behaviour: Sex-specific modulation of opioid- and endocannabinoid-related pathways.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Chronic migraine (CM) is a highly disabling condition that remains suboptimally treated. Metabolic disturbances may trigger migraine chronification, whereas impaired endogenous pain inhibition contributes to CM development. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), used for type 2 diabetes and obesity, show efficacy in chronic pain models. We evaluated the prophylactic effects of liraglutide, semaglutide and dulaglutide compared with propranolol (reference drug), potential opioidergic/endocannabinoid involvement and sex differences in a CM model. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Chronic migraine-like hypersensitivity was induced by repeated nitroglycerin administration in male and female mice. The prophylactic effects of GLP-1RAs and propranolol were examined using von Frey, acetone and orofacial glutamate tests. Body weight and glucose tolerance were monitored to evaluate metabolic safety. Potential opioidergic/endocannabinoid involvement in semaglutide-induced antinociception (selected GLP-1RA class representative) was assessed by pharmacological blockade and/or quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) analysis of pain-related neurobiomarker mRNA expression in brainstem and trigeminal ganglia. KEY RESULTS: Liraglutide, semaglutide and dulaglutide dose-dependently attenuated CM-like hypersensitivity in both sexes, with efficacy comparable to propranolol. GLP-1RAs did not affect metabolic parameters, whereas propranolol induced male-specific hyperglycaemia. Semaglutide-induced antinociception was partially sensitive to naloxone and was associated with sex-dimorphic, brainstem-specific transcriptional changes in opioid- and endocannabinoid-related pathways. Semaglutide increased Glp1r, Cnr1, Pomc, Pcsk1 and Pcsk2 mRNA expression in males, whereas it up-regulated Glp1r and down-regulated Faah and Mgll in females. CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: GLP-1RAs exert class-wide antinociceptive effects in a preclinical CM model, with semaglutide-based analyses suggesting sex-specific modulation of central opioid- and endocannabinoid-related pathways. These findings support further investigation of GLP-1RAs as prophylactic strategies for migraine, particularly in individuals with metabolic comorbidities.

articles.title: Fluoxetine attenuates asthma symptoms in a murine model through modulation of innate and adaptive immune components, and regulation of RORγt signalling axis in a pathogenic Th17 cell population.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Asthma is a heterogeneous chronic inflammatory airway disease, characterised by dysregulated interactions between innate and adaptive immune cells. Although Th2-mediated inflammation predominates, persistent Th17-associated immune responses contribute to chronic airway inflammation implicated in the corticosteroid-insensitive disease state. Fluoxetine, a SSRI with immunomodulatory properties, was investigated to determine its effects on inflammation and Th17 response in experimental allergic airway disease. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Immunomodulatory effects of fluoxetine evaluated in exploratory in vitro assays. In vivo studies were performed in an ovalbumin (OVA)-induced murine model of allergic asthma using oral fluoxetine at clinically relevant doses. Airway pathology, immunophenotypes, cytokine production, gene and protein expression were evaluated by histology, flow cytometry, quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR), confocal microscopy and ex vivo functional assays. Public transcriptomic datasets were integrated with target enrichment analyses, molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations used to explore potential molecular interactions. KEY RESULTS: Fluoxetine reduced the inflammatory response in activated macrophages without noticeable cytotoxicity. In an allergic asthma model, fluoxetine attenuated inflammatory cell infiltration, eosinophilia, IgE production and pulmonary macrophage activation, whilst reducing the accumulation of the phenotypically granulocytic myeloid-derived suppressor like cell population along with diminished T-cell activation and reduced Th17 responses, reduced IL-17 production together with decreased expression and nuclear localisation of RORγt. Ex vivo studies confirmed inhibition of RORγt expression and IL-17 production in Th17 cells. Transcriptomic integration identified significant enrichment of Th17-associated inflammatory pathways, whereas molecular docking and molecular dynamics analyses supported RORγt as a plausible molecular target. CONCLUSION AND IMPLICATIONS: Fluoxetine attenuates experimental allergic airway inflammation through coordinated modulation of innate and adaptive immune responses, with suppression of the RORγt-IL-17 signalling axis emerging as a key mechanistic feature. These findings expand the immunopharmacological profile of fluoxetine and provide an experimental rationale for further investigating its therapeutic potential in Th17-associated airway inflammatory diseases and in experimental models that more closely recapitulate corticosteroid-resistant asthma.

articles.title: Therapeutic targeting of the PRMT6/FOXK1 axis restores lipid homeostasis and ameliorates hepatic steatosis and steatohepatitis in mice.
articles.abstract: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is emerging as the leading cause of chronic liver disease, posing a global public health challenge without available therapeutic approaches. Protein arginine methyltransferase 6 is a type I PRMT that asymmetrically dimethylates arginine residues of a variety of substrates implicated in many diseases. However, its role in NAFLD pathologies has not been clarified. In this study, we show that PRMT6 is upregulated in NAFLD and NASH of mice and human patients. Prmt6-deficient mice are protected from diet-induced hepatic steatosis, steatohepatitis, insulin resistance, and glucose tolerance. Mechanistically, PRMT6 interacts with and dimethylates Forkhead box K1 (FOXK1) at four conserved arginine residues (R161, R191, R259, and R486), maintaining its nuclear localization and transcriptional activity as a repressor/activator, inhibiting fatty acid oxidation and stimulating lipogenesis programs, respectively. PRMT6 competes with glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK3) for binding to FOXK1 and triggers FOXK1 methylation. This methylation prevents FOXK1 from GSK3-mediated phosphorylation, leading to its dissociation from 14-3-3, enhanced nuclear retention, and transcriptional activity. Conversely, the methylation-defective FOXK1 mutant (4RK) has the opposite effect and confers resistance to diet-induced hepatic steatosis in mice. Moreover, pharmacological inhibition of PRMT6 by EPZ020411 ameliorates NAFLD progression in mice. Thus, our study demonstrates the PRMT6-FOXK1 axis as a critical regulator of NAFLD and that targeting PRMT6 represents a novel therapeutic intervention for NAFLD.

articles.title: In vivo validation of intramolecular bivalent glues targeting PSMA reveals potent and tissue-selective BRD4 degradation in prostate cancer.
articles.abstract: Various approaches have been explored to address the on-target, off-tissue toxicity of PROTACs and molecular glues, but most fall short in achieving robust in vivo selectivity and efficacy. In this study, we introduce a delivery strategy that enables tissue-selective deployment of an ultra-potent, picomolar-active DCAF16-recruiting intramolecular bivalent glue (IBG3) for BRD4 degradation in prostate cancer models by targeting the prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA). We first introduced rational modifications to IBG3 to install a suitable conjugation handle for PSMA ligand attachment, and incorporated a cathepsins-sensitive cleavable linker together with a dual functional polycarboxylate linker that enhances PSMA binding while suppressing passive diffusion. Selective BRD4 degradation was validated by multiple orthogonal assays in vitro and in vivo. The lead conjugate IBG-P3 achieved 79.8% tumor growth inhibition at 0.01 mg/kg in PC3-PIP xenografts, while an epimeric control lacking PSMA binding was inactive. Importantly, robust antitumor efficacy was further confirmed in an endogenous PSMA-expressing LNCaP xenograft model, where IBG-P3 achieved 72.6% tumor growth inhibition at a dose as low as 0.001 mg/kg, significantly outperforming the parent compound IBG3. This study provides the first in vivo validation of IBG degrader and establishes a preclinical framework for PSMA-guided delivery of potent degraders.

articles.title: Machine learning-driven discovery of aniline phenylacetate derivatives as LasR-targeted biofilm inhibitors against Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections.
articles.abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilm infections pose a severe clinical challenge due to antibiotic resistance driven by quorum sensing (QS). As the master regulator of the P. aeruginosa QS hierarchy, LasR controls biofilm initiation and key virulence factors, establishing it as a high-value therapeutic target. Here, we developed a machine learning pipeline integrating graph neural networks, pharmacophore modeling, molecular docking and molecular dynamics, and determined that the aniline-phenylacetic acid derivative (compound 2g) is an effective LasR inhibitor. 2g demonstrated exceptional biofilm inhibition (IC50 = 0.14 ± 0.08 μmol/L) without bactericidal activity (MIC >256 μmol/L). and bound LasR with high affinity (K D = 38.97 μmol/L). Mechanistically, transcriptomics revealed selective suppression of LasR-regulated virulence pathways, reducing pyocyanin production and bacterial motility. Notably, 2g synergized with antibiotics in vivo, reducing effective doses of ciprofloxacin and tobramycin by 1000-fold and 500-fold, respectively, while potently suppressing resistance evolution. Pharmacokinetic profiling further demonstrated favorable oral bioavailability (26.8%) and a wide safety margin. This work establishes 2g as a machine learning-optimized LasR inhibitor with potent antibiofilm activity and synergistic antibiotic enhancement, offering a translatable strategy against multidrug-resistant P. aeruginosa infections.

articles.title: Reprogramming gut microbiota and targeting CXCL1: The multifaceted mechanism of PLP1 in ameliorating alcohol-induced liver disease.
articles.abstract: Hepatic inflammation and gut barrier dysfunction are core pathologies of alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD), yet effective therapies remain limited. Pueraria lobata polysaccharide (PLP1), a key active constituent of P. lobata Radix, has demonstrated hepatoprotective potential; however, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this study, we sought to elucidate the therapeutic mechanism of PLP1 against experimental ALD by integrating proteomics, metabolomics, and gut microbiota analyses. We demonstrated that PLP1 initially functions through a microbiota-dependent pathway, transferable by fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), to restore gut barrier integrity and suppress the gut‒LPS‒TLR4 inflammatory axis. Furthermore, PLP1 exerted a direct, microbiota-independent effect, maintaining its therapeutic efficacy in antibiotic-depleted mice. Mechanistically, PLP1 directly and specifically targets CXCL1, promoting its ubiquitin-mediated proteasomal degradation as confirmed by biophysical assays. The functional necessity of this interaction was definitively established via comprehensive genetic manipulation of CXCL1 in vitro and in vivo. Specifically, CXCL1 overexpression reversed PLP1's benefits, whereas CXCL1 knockdown mimicked its effects and occluded any additional benefit from PLP1. Overall, PLP1 ameliorates ALD by independently targeting both extrinsic and intrinsic inflammatory triggers. This study reveals the multifaceted pharmacology of a natural polysaccharide and validates a dual-pronged therapeutic strategy for ALD.

articles.title: Remodeling macrophage efferocytosis and phenotype via targeted nanoimmunotherapy for atherosclerosis.
articles.abstract: Macrophages within advanced atherosclerotic lesions typically exhibit impaired efferocytosis and tend to adopt a pro-inflammatory M1-like phenotype, leading to the progression of atherosclerosis. Despite this challenge, the development of biocompatible nanotherapeutics capable of effectively remodeling macrophage efferocytosis and phenotype remains elusive. Here, we developed engineered targeted-peptide-modified nanocarriers (PP) and demonstrated their potential to restore macrophage efferocytosis while promoting re-polarization towards an anti-inflammatory M2-like phenotype. Furthermore, PP efficiently facilitated the delivery of an inflammation-resolving-drug to lesional macrophages within advanced atherosclerotic lesions. This combination approach substantially enhanced the anti-atherosclerotic efficacy of PP-based nanomedicine, effectively ameliorating atherosclerosis progression. In advanced plaque-bearing ApoE -/- mice, PP nanomedcine efficiently accumulated in atherosclerotic plaques, notably restoring macrophage efferocytosis, promoting anti-inflammatory M2-like macrophage polarization, and leading to reduced plaque areas and enhanced plaque stability. This study not only underscores the new pleiotropic effects of PP to restore macrophage efferocytosis and modulate macrophage phenotype, but also highlights the promising potential of PP for the treatment of atherosclerosis and diseases associated with macrophage dysfunction.

articles.title: Unnatural amino acid-based miniPROTACs enable efficient oncoprotein degradation.
articles.abstract: Proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) harness the cell's proteolytic systems to eliminate harmful proteins for therapeutic purposes. Unnatural amino acids (UAAs) offer unique structural features for drug design but have not yet been applied to targeted protein degradation. Here, we develop a set of linker-free PROTACs in which Lys-derived UAAs-ornithine (Orn) and 2,4-diaminobutyric acid (Dab)-serve as degrons that are directly conjugated to target ligands, yielding compact and effective degraders. Both Orn-BA and Dab-BA promote the efficient degradation of EML4-ALK, with Dab-BA exhibiting superior potency, attributed to its enhanced ability to promote ternary complex formation with the target and E3 ligase. Dab-BA also significantly suppresses tumor growth in a xenograft mouse model. The general applicability of this UAA-based linker-free PROTAC approach is further demonstrated by the development of BCR-ABL degraders. Our study represents the first application of UAAs in targeted protein degradation and offers a complementary strategy for E3 ligand discovery.

articles.title: Antihypertensive drug-induced liver injury is rare, but strongly associated with HLA-B∗35:01.
articles.abstract: Anti-hypertensive (anti-HTN) drugs are widely prescribed, but the features of associated drug-induced liver injury (DILI) are poorly defined. A total of 2207 patients enrolled in the Drug-Induced Liver Injury Network (DILIN) from 2003 to 2024 were adjudicated as definite, highly likely, or probable DILI. Of these, 44 cases were attributed to anti-HTN drugs. These were compared with non-anti-HTN DILI cases and population controls. Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) sequencing was performed, and allele frequencies were analyzed using Fisher's Exact Test. Among the 44 anti-HTN DILI cases, 14 were caused by ACE inhibitors/ARBs, 13 by methyldopa, 11 by hydralazine, and 3 each by beta-blockers and calcium-channel blockers. Methyldopa DILI presented with hepatocellular injury in young women (prescribed mainly for pregnancy-related HTN). Non-methyldopa cases were 60% hepatocellular, 28% cholestatic, and 9% mixed. Severe outcomes included two liver transplants and two deaths (lisinopril and hydralazine). HLA-B∗35:01 was markedly enriched (50% vs. 13% in controls; OR 6.0; P = 1 × 10-8) and was linked to shorter latency (50 vs. 109 days; P = 0.02) but not severity. HLA-B∗35:01 was overrepresented across all drug classes, including 66% of methyldopa cases, 27% of hydralazine cases, and 42% of ACE/ARB cases. DILI from anti-HTN medications is very rare but strongly associated with HLA-B∗35:01, especially for methyldopa. Carriers display a shorter latency, potentially indicating an accelerated adaptive immune response, that warrants further exploration.

articles.title: Effects of anti-PEG antibodies on extravascular transport of stealth liposome: A study on interspecies differences.
articles.abstract: Cutaneous toxicity of stealth liposomal doxorubicin (sLip/DOX) has been attributed to the phagocytosis and extravascular transport of the liposomal carrier into skin by circulating neutrophils, which depended on the complement-mediated opsonization. As potent triggers of complement activation, anti-polyethylene glycol (PEG) antibodies may critically influence the cutaneous accumulation of liposomes, which has not been systematically investigated. Moreover, interspecies variability complicates the preclinical evaluation and prediction of liposomal toxicity. To bridge this gap, the present work evaluated the effects of anti-PEG antibody on the extravascular transport of stealth liposome (sLip) from an interspecies perspective. The study also investigated how anti-PEG antibody-mediated complement activation differentially shapes the cutaneous distribution dynamics and spatial accumulation patterns of liposomal drugs across species. Strikingly, mice exhibited increased skin accumulation and toxicity in the presence of anti-PEG antibody, whereas rats showed reduced cutaneous exposure due to predominant hepatic-splenic clearance. Collectively, our findings suggested that interspecies physiological variabilities determine the in vivo fate of sLip and provided mechanistic insights for predicting and mitigating liposomal toxicities in translational settings.

articles.title: In vivo fate mapping of a paclitaxel-loaded polymeric micelle and its components.
articles.abstract: Paclitaxel (PTX) has poor aqueous solubility and vehicle-related toxicity. Polymeric micelles (PMs) can improve solubility and leverage the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect for tumor targeting. However, a comprehensive understanding of their in vivo fate remains limited, due to the inability to distinguish between encapsulated and released drug. We developed a novel method integrating stable isotope tracing, ultrafiltration, and ultra-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS) to quantify free, released, and total PTX, the polymeric carriers methoxy-poly(ethylene glycol) (molecular weight ∼2000 Da) (mPEG2K) and methoxy-poly(ethylene glycol)-block-poly(d,l-lactic acid) (mPEG block MW ∼2000 Da, PLA block MW ∼2000 Da) (mPEG2K-PLA2K) in rats following administration of PTX injection and paclitaxel-loaded polymeric micelles (PTX-PMs). PTX-PMs significantly altered the pharmacokinetics, reducing the initial dose-normalized initial plasma concentration (C 0/Dose) of free PTX to 27.0% of that from the injection. Altered tissue distribution was observed, with high accumulation in reticuloendothelial system (RES) organs and more complete clearance by 48 h. Excretion studies revealed a substantially higher cumulative fecal excretion of PTX after PTX-PMs administration, while the polymer carrier was predominantly excreted renally as mPEG2K. These findings provide critical insights into the in vivo disposition of PTX nanoformulations, supporting the rational design of PMs-based delivery systems.

articles.title: Molecular mechanisms of YZG-331 ameliorated insomnia based on the gut microbiota-drug interaction.
articles.abstract: The gut microbiota plays a crucial role in the study of drug efficacy and metabolism. YZG-331 exhibits significant sedative and hypnotic effects. However, the oral bioavailability of YZG-331 in female mice remains low at 27.7%, and it exhibits instability in the gut microbiota, undergoing rapid metabolism, with the intestinal hydrolytic metabolite M2 identified as the characteristic metabolite. Both the underlying mechanisms of YZG-331 therapeutic effects on insomnia and its enzyme-mediated metabolic pathways involving the gut microbiota remain incompletely elucidated. In this study, we found that YZG-331 regulated the tryptophan metabolism and 5-HT production pathways by the gut microbiota. Specifically, YZG-331 increased the abundance of Lactobacillus and Muribaculaceae in the gut, with Lactobacillus reuteri playing a critical role in both the metabolic processes of YZG-331 and the biosynthesis of tryptophan-derived metabolites. YZG-331 enhanced the activation of the tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) cofactor system, which subsequently promoted tryptophan hydroxylase (TPH) activity, thereby enhancing 5-HT production. Furthermore, YZG-331 and M2 increased intestinal butyric acid levels, thereby promoting sleep regulation and supporting the restoration of the intestinal barrier. Overall, our study provided the first evidence highlighting the crucial role of the gut microbiota in the therapeutic mechanism and metabolic processing of YZG-331 in the treatment of insomnia.

articles.title: Lysosomal membrane damage repair and acidification impairment restoration triggered by smart lipid nanoparticles for Alzheimer's disease treatment.
articles.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD), characterized by amyloid (Aβ) deposition in neurons, is the most serious neurodegenerative disorder, but lacks effective therapeutic drugs in the clinic. Impaired neuronal lysosomal function drives the pathological accumulation of intracellular Aβ. Targeted rehabilitation of lysosomal dysfunction may offer a potential strategy to restore neuronal homeostasis and mitigate AD progression. In this study, we developed a brain-targeted smart lipid nanoparticle (A-PSL@7BIO) to repair lysosomal membrane damage and restore impaired acidification in the brain for AD therapy. The system was composed of Angiopep-2 peptide-conjugated lipid nanoparticles, which were loaded with a Glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β) inhibitor 7-bromoindirubin-3'-oxime (7BIO) and incorporated with dipalmitoyl-phosphatidylserine (DPPS) and a reactive oxygen species (ROS) responsive phospholipid. Through Angiopep-2-mediated blood-brain barrier (BBB) transcytosis, the smart lipid nanoparticles could enhance brain biodistribution with subsequent neuronal internalization. Pathologically elevated intracellular ROS levels in AD could induce stimulus-responsive payload release, wherein 7BIO selectively inhibited aberrant GSK-3β hyperphosphorylation to restore the physiological acidic lysosomal environment and DPPS structurally repaired compromised lysosomal membranes, synergistically addressing dual aspects of lysosomal pathology. This smart lipid nanoparticles synergistically restored physiological lysosomal homeostasis, reversed neuronal dysfunction, and ameliorated cognitive deficits in AD models, indicating that A-PSL@7BIO could be used as a potential nanomedicine for AD therapy.

articles.title: Stimulate-and-retain hydrogel strategy integrating oncolytic virus and oxaliplatin for dual ICD-inducing antitumor immunity.
articles.abstract: Immunogenic cell death (ICD) provides a promising strategy for cancer treatment by stimulating anti-tumor immunity. However, single ICD inducers often elicit insufficient damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), and the rapid clearance of these DAMPs at the tumor site further prevents sustained immune stimulation. To address these challenges, we developed a polyphenol-based bioadhesive hydrogel antigen reservoir functionalized with dopamine (DA) and loaded with dual ICD inducers. Specifically, thymidine kinase (tk)-deficient oncolytic vaccinia virus (VV, a type II ICD inducer) was combined with oxaliplatin (OXA, a type I ICD inducer), thereby enhancing direct tumor cytotoxicity and synergistically amplifying ICD through distinct mechanisms to promote robust DAMP release. Subsequently, the released DAMPs were captured and retained by the DA-functionalized hyaluronic acid-Pluronic® F127 hydrogel (HADP), forming an antigen reservoir at the tumor site. This synergistic "stimulate-and-retain" strategy not only augments ICD-mediated DAMP release but also prolongs their local availability to sustain immune stimulation. In murine models, the OXA-HADP@VV facilitated dendritic cell (DC) activation, increased IFN-γ +CD8+ T cell infiltration, and reduced regulatory T cells (Tregs), thereby achieving effective tumor suppression and strong anti-recurrence effects. Together, this dual ICD-inducing antigen reservoir provides a versatile platform for improving cancer immunotherapy.

articles.title: The role of cardiomyocytic FOXP3 and extracellular vesicle-mediated delivery of FOXP3 into cardiomyocytes for treating pathological cardiac hypertrophy.
articles.abstract: While forkhead helix transcription factor P3 (FOXP3) is a key regulator in T cells, we previously reported its anti-hypertrophic role in cardiomyocytes. In the present study, by overexpressing FOXP3 and using RNA-seq, we found that FOXP3 suppresses pathological cardiac hypertrophy by upregulating ferritin heavy chain 1, thereby inhibiting ferroptosis. However, data from the single-RNA sequence database showed that the in vivo cardiomyocytes exhibit minimal Foxp3 mRNA, despite the presence of FOXP3 protein. Here, we identified cardiac microenvironment-derived extracellular vesicles (cEVs) carrying FOXP3 protein as the source of cardiomyocytic FOXP3. Leveraging this intercellular delivery mechanism, we demonstrate that administering FOXP3+ cEVs from healthy hearts mitigates isoproterenol (ISO)-induced ferroptosis and hypertrophy. Due to the impracticality of large-scale production of cEVs, we identified the Jurkat cell as an alternative source of FOXP3+ EVs. The Jurkat cell-derived EVs (jEVs) increased the content of cardiomyocytic FOXP3, thereby reversing hypertrophic responses. Moreover, we engineered Jurkat cells to increase FOXP3 content in the jEVs, thereby obtaining FOXP3-enriched jEVs that exhibited superior attenuation of hypertrophy and suppression of ferroptosis compared to native EVs. These findings suggest that increasing the content of FOXP3 protein in cardiomyocytes through engineered FOXP3-enriched extracellular vesicles offers a novel strategy for treating cardiac hypertrophy.

articles.title: Discovery of a potent covalent inhibitor for the treatment of sepsis targeting DNAJC9: Identification of a druggable target for inflammation.
articles.abstract: Sepsis is a leading cause of mortality among patients in intensive care units (ICUs), with no specific treatments for sepsis available in clinical practice. In this study, we report the discovery of compound A12, a tanshinone derivative featuring a covalent warhead, which demonstrates potent anti-inflammatory effects both in vitro and in vivo. In a lipopolysaccharide-induced mouse model of endotoxemia and acute systemic inflammation, A12 significantly reduces levels of TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-12. Distinct from current anti-inflammatory small molecules, A12 presents a unique mechanism, covalently binding to DNAJC9, thereby modulating the HSP complex and inhibiting the downstream inflammatory response. This work represents the first application of covalent drug design principles to the structural modification of the natural product tanshinone, and reveals the previously unrecognized role of DNAJC9 in inflammatory diseases, offering a novel therapeutic target for management of sepsis-associated acute systemic inflammation.

articles.title: Identification and characterization of a non-nucleotide RdRp allosteric inhibitor with pan-coronavirus protection.
articles.abstract: The viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) is a conserved and compelling target for pan-coronavirus antiviral development. To date, all US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved RdRp inhibitors are nucleotide inhibitors (NIs), which are prone to drug resistance and show limited clinical efficacy. Developing alternative non-nucleotide inhibitors (NNIs) with high target specificity, structural diversity, and metabolic stability could yield more effective antivirals. Here, we identify an allosteric RdRp NNI, BAY-850, via computational screening. BAY-850 exhibits potent, broad-spectrum antiviral activity against multiple SARS-CoV-2 variants and other human coronaviruses. Mechanistic studies show that BAY-850 binds directly to a previously unrecognized allosteric site on nsp12, thereby fine-tuning the catalytic motif F loop out-conformation the orthosteric site. Importantly, therapeutic administration of BAY-850 significantly reduces viral loads in the nasal turbinates and lungs of SARS-CoV-2-infected K18-hACE2 mice. These findings validate a novel allosteric site in RdRp and support BAY-850 as a start-point for broad-spectrum anti-coronavirus development.

articles.title: Oral artificial microbio-vaccine triggers synergistic immunogenic cell death induction and tumor microenvironment remodeling for liver cancer therapy.
articles.abstract: Artificial cellular systems, engineered to mimic biological functions, offer a promising platform for advanced drug delivery and immunotherapy. Translating such systems into effective oral tumor vaccines, however, remains challenging due to the harsh gastrointestinal environment, inefficient immune activation, and the toxicity of potent immunogenic agents. To overcome these barriers, we engineered an oral artificial micro bio-vaccine via a hierarchical assembly strategy. Triptolide (TP), an immunogenic cell death inducer, was co-assembled with glycyrrhizic acid (GA), an immunomodulator, into a nanodetoxifying core to facilitate efficient loading into hollow Saccharomyces cerevisiae microcapsules (YC), forming the final aggregate (TP/GA-NYPs). This rational design leverages the YC for gastric protection and gut mucosa-targeting, while the Chitosan shell ensures robust encapsulation. Crucially, the TP/GA core demonstrates a synergistic interplay, in which TP potently induces immunogenic cell death, while GA concurrently remodels the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment by suppressing metastasis-related markers and enhancing immunostimulatory cytokine profiles. This spatiotemporally coupled action within a single oral aggregate elicits robust intestinal mucosal and systemic immunity, effectively suppressing liver cancer progression and metastasis while mitigating the systemic toxicity of TP. This work highlights the therapeutic potential of functional aggregates in orchestrating synergistic anti-tumor immunity and offers a versatile platform for oral immunotherapy.

articles.title: BD2-selective BRD4 inhibitor ZX29 mitigates myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury via BRD4-YY1-NCOA4 axis disruption and ferroptosis inhibition.
articles.abstract: Myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury (MI/RI) remains a major barrier to ischemic heart disease treatment, as reperfusion therapies often exacerbate cardiac damage. Bromodomain-containing protein 4 (BRD4) is a key epigenetic target in cardiovascular diseases, but pan-BRD4 inhibitors cause severe off-target toxicity by disrupting basal bromodomain 1 (BD1) function, highlighting the need for BD2-selective agents. This study aimed to develop a BD2-selective BRD4 inhibitor and clarify its mechanism. ZX29 was developed via virtual screening of 100,000 compounds and structure-based optimization, exhibiting potent BRD4 binding with an IC50 of 0.27 ± 0.03 μmol/L and K d of 1.68 μmol/L, outperforming clinical agent RVX-208. ZX29 specifically binds BRD4 BD2 via H437/V439 residues. In murine MI/RI models, oral ZX29 significantly improved cardiac systolic and diastolic function, reduced myocardial infarct size, and mitigated lipid peroxidation. Mechanistically, ZX29 disrupted the BRD4-Yin Yang 1 (YY1) interaction and inhibited the nuclear receptor coactivator 4 (NCOA4)-ferritin heavy chain 1 (FTH1) degradation axis, suppressing lysosomal ferrous iron release and ferroptosis. Moreover, ZX29 preserved mitochondrial function by maintaining mitochondrial membrane potential and boosting ATP production. Ultimately, this study validates selective BRD4 BD2 inhibition as a safe and effective therapeutic strategy for MI/RI and establishes ZX29 as a viable clinical candidate.

articles.title: Selenium nanozymes effectively treat rheumatoid arthritis by specifically activating selenoproteins to block oxidative damage and cGAS-STING signaling pathway.
articles.abstract: Redox imbalance has become an important factor in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) progression, previous studies showed selenium nanozymes (Se NPs) effectively treated RA by restoring redox. However, the process of Se NPs regulates RA, especially the mechanism of Se NPs activates selenoproteins in inhibiting inflammation remains unclear. Herein, the redox imbalance in RA patients was first analyzed, and selenoproteins associated with macrophage inflammation were identified via mRNA profiling. Subsequently, the synthesized Se NPs with glutathione peroxidase (GPX)-like activity as a supplement, and it was found that Se NPs specially upregulate selenoproteins in macrophages applied to in vitro and in vivo models, furthermore combined with GPX-like activity, Se NPs quickly eliminated reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (RONS), restored redox homeostasis in RA, and alleviated symptoms of RA by effectively inhibiting macrophage inflammation. The mechanistic study showed that Se NPs effectively prevent mitochondrial and nDNA damage by specifically activating selenoproteins, blocking the interaction between DNA and cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS), and restraining the activation of cGAS-stimulator of interferon genes (STING) and nuclear factor kappa-B (NF-κB) pathway, thus effectively suppressing macrophage inflammation and treating RA. Therefore, this study reveals the mechanism by which Se NPs inhibit macrophage inflammation, providing a new potential therapeutic target for treating inflammatory diseases.

articles.title: Double coordination-driven Fe-DOX synergy enhances ferroptosis and immunogenic cancer therapy.
